title: Industrial ambition without institutional transformation: Africa’s industrial policy challenge
body:
It is no longer news that industrial policy is back on the global development agenda.

After decades of market fundamentalism, even advanced economies are now openly deploying industrial policy to secure supply chains, accelerate green transitions, and rebuild strategic industries.

Africa is understandably responding to this moment. But is it on the right path?

Across the continent, national governments are advancing industrial ambitions tied to green minerals, battery value chains, pharmaceuticals, agro-processing, manufacturing, and renewable energy.

- These efforts are in the right direction. However, there has been little corresponding transformation in the underlying institutional architecture.
- This reflects a persistent, but erroneous, assumption that industrial policy is automatically developmental.

Consider three possible scenarios.

The developmental pathway: Industrial policy is tied to clear performance targets, learning incentives, and accountability mechanisms. Firms receiving support are expected to upgrade, innovate, and scale production.

- Under this scenario, industrial policy becomes a vehicle for capability building and structural transformation.

The distributive pathway: Support is allocated through political proximity rather than productive potential. Subsidies and incentives become instruments of patronage.

- Under this scenario, industrial policy reproduces rent-seeking and protects inefficient incumbents instead of upgrading industries.

The extractive continuity pathway

Industrial policy exists on paper, but the economy remains locked into raw commodity exports. Minerals are extracted, value is exported, and domestic production systems fail to deepen.

- Under this scenario, the language of industrialization advances, but the structure of dependency remains intact.

**Implication:** Industrial policy does not produce transformation simply because governments announce incentives, establish industrial parks, or publish strategic plans.

Without institutions capable of disciplining capital, coordinating investment, monitoring performance, and institutionalizing learning, industrial policy can easily become a mechanism for rent distribution rather than productive transformation.

This shifts the debate from policy design alone to institutional transformation and state capacity building as the future of Africa’s industrialization will likely be shaped by which of the scenarios described above becomes dominant.

**Bottom Line:** Africa does not merely need industrial ambition. It needs State and institutions capable of converting ambition into production. This is where the continent’s real frontier of industrial transformation lies.

Industrial policy succeeds not because it exists, but because it is governed well.
